reels.topic: Code of ethics: the four canons
reels.source: D1_L02_Professional_Ethics_script.md
reels.hook: Your boss says: hide the flaw.

segments.say: Your boss asks you to hide a known safety flaw from customers. What does a C I S S P do?
segments.show: Your boss asks you to hide a known safety flaw from customers. What does a CISSP do?

segments.say: The code of ethics has four canons... in priority order.
segments.show: The code of ethics has four canons, in priority order.

segments.say: One. Protect society, the common good, public trust, and the infrastructure.
segments.show: 1. Protect society, the common good, public trust and the infrastructure.

segments.say: Two. Act honorably, honestly, justly, responsibly, and legally.
segments.show: 2. Act honorably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally.

segments.say: Three. Provide diligent and competent service to principals... that's your employer.
segments.show: 3. Provide diligent and competent service to principals (your employer).

segments.say: Four. Advance and protect the profession.
segments.show: 4. Advance and protect the profession.

segments.say: Serving your employer is canon three. Protecting society is canon one... and the higher canon always wins. So you don't hide it.
segments.show: Serving your employer is canon 3. Protecting society is canon 1. The higher canon wins, so you don't hide it.

segments.say: Follow for more C I S S P prep.
segments.show: Follow for more CISSP prep.

post.title: Your boss says hide the flaw. What does a CISSP do? #Shorts
post.caption: The CISSP code of ethics has four canons, applied in priority order. Protecting society (canon 1) beats serving your employer (canon 3). Learn the order for exam day.

reels.topic: SLE, ARO and ALE worked example
reels.source: D1_L10_Risk_Management_I_Terms_Analysis_script.md
reels.hook: The one risk formula you must know

segments.say: One formula every C I S S P must know. Let's do it in thirty seconds.
segments.show: One formula every CISSP must know. Let's do it in 30 seconds.

segments.say: A server is worth one hundred thousand dollars.
segments.show: A server is worth $100,000.

segments.say: A flood would destroy forty percent of it. That's the exposure factor.
segments.show: A flood would destroy 40% of it. That's the exposure factor.

segments.say: So the single loss expectancy, S L E, is forty thousand dollars.
segments.show: So the single loss expectancy (SLE) is $40,000.

segments.say: A flood is expected once every ten years. So the annualized rate of occurrence, A R O, is zero point one.
segments.show: A flood is expected once every 10 years, so the annualized rate of occurrence (ARO) is 0.1.

segments.say: Annualized loss expectancy, A L E, equals S L E times A R O... four thousand dollars a year.
segments.show: Annualized loss expectancy (ALE) = SLE × ARO = $4,000 a year.

segments.say: So a safeguard against this flood should never cost more than four thousand dollars a year. Save this one.
segments.show: A safeguard against this flood should never cost more than $4,000 a year. Save this one.

segments.say: Follow for more C I S S P prep.
segments.show: Follow for more CISSP prep.

post.title: SLE × ARO = ALE in 30 seconds (CISSP risk math) #Shorts
post.caption: $100,000 asset × 40% exposure factor = $40,000 SLE. × 0.1 ARO = $4,000 ALE. Never spend more per year on a safeguard than the annual loss it prevents.

segments.say: The C I S S P isn't testing whether you can fix the server. It's testing how you think.

segments.say: Rule one. Human safety comes first. Before data, before systems.

segments.say: Rule two. Senior management owns the risk. Security advises... management decides.

segments.say: Rule three. Pick the answer that fixes the root cause... not just the symptom.
